3. Download the documents

Using Part B of govtdata01.R, download the ten most recent hearings of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations.


library(httr2)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)
library(readr)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

key <- Sys.getenv("GOVINFO_API_KEY")

if (!nzchar(key)) {
  stop("GOVINFO_API_KEY is missing.")
}

n_target <- 10
max_candidates <- 100
page_size <- 25

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Base API request
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

govinfo <- function(path) {
  request(paste0("https://api.govinfo.gov/", path)) |>
    req_url_query(api_key = key) |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 3)
}

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Search Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearings
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

search_page <- function(offset = "*") {

  govinfo("search") |>
    req_body_json(list(
      query = paste(
        "collection:CHRG",
        "AND chamber:senate",
        'AND committee:("foreign relations")'
      ),
      pageSize = page_size,
      offsetMark = offset,
      sorts = list(
        list(
          field = "publishdate",
          sortOrder = "DESC"
        )
      )
    )) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_json()
}

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Retrieve package metadata
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

get_summary <- function(id) {

  tryCatch({

    govinfo(paste0("packages/", id, "/summary")) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()

  }, error = function(e) {

    warning(
      "Could not retrieve package ", id,
      ": ", conditionMessage(e)
    )

    NULL
  })
}

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Search for ten qualifying hearings
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

selected_hearings <- list()
seen <- character()
offset <- "*"

while (
  length(selected_hearings) < n_target &&
  length(seen) < max_candidates
) {

  page <- search_page(offset)

  results <- page$results

  if (is.null(results) || length(results) == 0) {
    break
  }

  # Process search results
  for (result in results) {

    if (
      length(selected_hearings) >= n_target ||
      length(seen) >= max_candidates
    ) {
      break
    }

    id <- result$packageId

    if (
      is.null(id) ||
      !nzchar(id) ||
      id %in% seen
    ) {
      next
    }

    seen <- c(seen, id)

    # Senate hearing package IDs contain "shrg"
    if (!grepl("^CHRG-[0-9]+shrg", id, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
      next
    }

    # Retrieve metadata
    summary <- get_summary(id)

    Sys.sleep(0.5)

    if (is.null(summary)) {
      next
    }

    # Retain qualifying hearing
    selected_hearings[[id]] <- summary

    # Progress reporting
    cat(
      "Examined:", length(seen),
      "| Found:", length(selected_hearings),
      "of", n_target, "\n"
    )

    if (length(selected_hearings) >= n_target) {
      break
    }
  }

  # Stop if complete or capped
  if (
    length(selected_hearings) >= n_target ||
    length(seen) >= max_candidates
  ) {
    break
  }

  # Move to next page
  next_offset <- page$offsetMark

  if (
    is.null(next_offset) ||
    identical(next_offset, offset)
  ) {
    break
  }

  offset <- next_offset
}

# Initialize with required columns to prevent empty-table errors
hearing_tbl <- tibble(
  packageId = character(),
  title = character(),
  dateIssued = character(),
  heldDates = character(),
  pdfLink = character(),
  txtLink = character(),
  modsLink = character()
)

# Extract metadata
if (length(selected_hearings) > 0) {

  hearing_tbl <- map_dfr(selected_hearings, \(s) {

    download <- s$download

    if (is.null(download)) {
      download <- list()
    }

    # Hearing summaries often list only premisLink, zipLink and modsLink
    # (see section 2c), so fall back to the package content endpoints,
    # which serve the PDF and HTML text for every package.
    pkg_url <- paste0("https://api.govinfo.gov/packages/", s$packageId)

    tibble(
      packageId = s$packageId %||% NA_character_,
      title = s$title %||% NA_character_,
      dateIssued = s$dateIssued %||% NA_character_,
      heldDates = paste(
        unlist(s$heldDates),
        collapse = "; "
      ),
      pdfLink = download$pdfLink %||% paste0(pkg_url, "/pdf"),
      txtLink = download$txtLink %||% paste0(pkg_url, "/htm"),
      modsLink = download$modsLink %||% paste0(pkg_url, "/mods")
    )
  })
}

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Results
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

# Output locations
pdf_dir <- "govinfo_pdfs"
log_file <- "assign05_download_log.csv"

dir.create(pdf_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Add PDF directory to .gitignore
gitignore <- ".gitignore"

existing_ignore <- if (file.exists(gitignore)) {
  readLines(gitignore, warn = FALSE)
} else {
  character()
}

if (!"govinfo_pdfs/" %in% existing_ignore) {
  cat("\ngovinfo_pdfs/\n", file = gitignore, append = TRUE)
}

# Download function
download_pdf <- function(id, url) {

  dest <- file.path(pdf_dir, paste0(id, ".pdf"))

  started <- format(
    Sys.time(),
    "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z"
  )

  if (is.na(url) || !nzchar(url)) {

    result <- list(
      status = "no pdfLink",
      http = NA_integer_,
      error = NA_character_
    )

  } else {

    result <- tryCatch({

      response <- request(url) |>
        req_url_query(api_key = key) |>
        req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
        req_perform(path = dest)

      list(
        status = "ok",
        http = resp_status(response),
        error = NA_character_
      )

    }, error = function(e) {

      list(
        status = "failed",
        http = NA_integer_,
        error = conditionMessage(e)
      )
    })
  }

  # Pause between downloads
  Sys.sleep(runif(1, 1, 3))

  tibble(
    packageId = id,
    pdf_url = url,
    file = dest,
    status = result$status,
    http_status = result$http,
    bytes = if (result$status == "ok") {
      file.size(dest)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    },
    error = result$error,
    started = started
  )
}

# Download all ten hearings
download_log <- map2_dfr(
  hearing_tbl$packageId,
  hearing_tbl$pdfLink,
  download_pdf
) |>
  left_join(
    hearing_tbl |>
      select(packageId, title, dateIssued),
    by = "packageId"
  )

# Save CSV log
write_csv(download_log, log_file)

# Display summary
cat("PDFs downloaded successfully:",
    sum(download_log$status == "ok"), "\n")

text:
4. Report
Write a short report on the difficulties you met.

How usable are the downloaded documents as data? What would it take to turn ten PDFs into a table or a corpus?

The PDFs are useful as sources but are not immediately useable for quantitative analysis. Converting them into a corpus would require extracting the text, removing formatting artifacts, and standardizing the documents. Scanned PDFs may also require OCR. Creating a structured table would require identifying fields such as hearing dates, committee names, speakers, and testimony, then validating the extracted information. This may currently be possible with some AI models.

How would you improve the process? Consider the other formats in download, and what the metadata gives you without opening a file.

The process could be improved by downloading text or XML files rather than PDFs if available. These formats are easier to parse and would reduce the need for text extraction or OCR. The API metadata already provides information such as titles, dates, IDs, and links, which allows the documents to be indexed and filtered. The main difficulties encountered were handling nested JSON responses, identifying the correct committee hearings, and managing pagination.
The largest problem was that the package summaries for these hearings listed only premisLink, zipLink and modsLink, with no pdfLink, so the first run downloaded nothing. Requesting each package’s PDF directly from /packages/{packageId}/pdf fixed it.

In two sentences: what did the API give you that the search page and last week’s scraping did not?

The API provided structured, machine-readable results. The API allowed direct access to document metadata and download links.

Never print the key, never put it in a .qmd, and if you keep a .Renviron inside your website folder, add it to .gitignore first: the repository is public.

title: EPPS 6302 Methods of Data Collection and Production: Prepare for Class 9
section: 5. Discuss — a comment section as data
text:
5. Discuss — a comment section as data

Who writes YouTube comments, and who reads them? Who never appears?
What edits them — channel moderation, held-for-review filters, YouTube’s ranking (order = "relevance"), deletions?
What selects the comments you can collect: the search ranking, the video, the channel, your max_results, the day you ran it?
The API terms allow you to keep this data 30 days. What does that mean for reproducibility — and for your website?


a. Who writes, who reads, who never appears
A small, self-selected minority writes comments, and a few accounts write most of them. Commenters lean toward people with strong views, and they include spam accounts, bots, coordinated campaigns, and the channel owner. Many more people read than write. Most viewers never comment, so the comment section measures the engaged tail, not the audience.
Several groups never appear:

Viewers who watch silently.
People who don’t use YouTube at all. They skew older and toward places with poor broadband, which matters for a siting question.
Anyone whose comment was removed or held.
Every viewer of a video with comments disabled. Made-for-Kids videos have comments turned off automatically.

For your project, the people who live next to a proposed facility may be far less visible than national commentators. Because comments carry no location, you can’t tell the two apart.


b. What edits them
Comments pass through several filters before you see them:

The commenter: People edit their own comments, which is why updated_at exists.
The creator: Creators can delete comments, hide users, block words, and hold comments for review. Held comments aren’t public, so the API never returns them.
YouTube: Automated spam filters hold comments, and policy enforcement removes them.
Ranking: The call above uses the API default, order = "time", so truncation favors recent comment threads. If order = "relevance" is requested, truncation favors comments YouTube ranks as relevant.
Partial replies: commentThreads.list returns top-level threads and may include only some replies. A fuller collection would follow up with comments.list for replies.
Timing: Deletion can happen after you collect a comment. A stored corpus can therefore contain comments that are no longer public, which matters for (d).



c. What selects what you can collect
Each layer narrows the sample:

Search: search.list returns a relevance-ranked sample, not a complete list. It is shaped by the query, regionCode, relevanceLanguage, pagination, and the day of collection.
The video and channel: Their audience, moderation norms, and whether comments are enabled all shape what is available.
max_results and paging: With the default time ordering, stopping after 100 selects recent top-level threads, not a random 100. With relevance ordering, it selects the threads YouTube ranks most highly.
The day you ran it: Comments keep arriving, and some get edited or deleted. nrow(cmts) can differ from get_video_stats() because the former counts retrieved top-level threads and the latter reports a broader total that includes replies.
Quota: Quota and endpoint-specific call limits constrain how much can be collected.

For this exercise, the corpus is a sample of publicly visible top-level comments, at the time of collection, on the latest upload from one fixed channel. In a search-based project, YouTube’s ranking of videos adds another selection layer. Neither corpus is a sample of public opinion; its frame is defined by the query or channel, video-selection rule, API filters, collection time, and result limit.


d. The 30-day rule: reproducibility and your website
Section III.E.4 of the policy is specific:

Data collected with only an API key is “Non-Authorized Data.”
You may store limited amounts of it temporarily, for no more than 30 days. After that you must delete it or refresh it.
The same limit applies to statistics like view counts and subscriber counts.
Stored data must reasonably match what YouTube currently shows.

Three consequences:

You can’t publish a frozen comment corpus for others to rerun. Reproducibility moves from sharing data to sharing code, queries, collection dates, and a clear description of the sampling process.
Re-collection won’t match exactly. Re-pulling the same IDs later can return a different set because comments are added, deleted, or edited.
The research design is affected. A plan for frozen, hashed weekly snapshots or a sealed estimation sample conflicts with the 30-day refresh-or-delete rule for Non-Authorized Data. Section III.E.4.h also restricts derived metrics from API data. The project should confirm what is permitted under the applicable terms or a research authorization before retaining long-term snapshots or publishing derived scores.

For the website:

Keep Parquet files and raw comment text out of the public repository with .gitignore.
Check rendered output carefully: Quarto’s _freeze folder and rendered HTML can preserve printed comment text or API statistics.
Publish the collection code, queries, dates, and sampling description. Publish aggregate or derived results only after confirming that the applicable YouTube terms or research authorization permit them.

Sources:
(YouTube API Services – Developer Policies (§III.E.4, §III.E.6; last updated 2026-10-15))

A small, documented collection of YouTube videos and comments on the 2026 US midterm elections — made with an API key and a quota plan, before and after Election Day (3 November); a quanteda analysis of the comments by channel; and a short report on what a comment section is a sample of, compared with the tweets and presidential documents of Assignment 6.







How this page renders

b. Find the videos — twice (Part 3a). Search "US midterm election" for videos published 1 September – 27 October 2026, once with order = "relevance" and once with order = "viewCount" (100 results each).


run_search <- function(order, after, before) {
  yt_search(term             = search_term,
            published_after  = after,
            published_before = before,
            order            = order,
            max_results      = n_search)
}

# i-iii: overlap, reported vs. returned, duplicates
summarise_search <- function(s, period) {
  imap(s, \(x, ord) tibble(
    period         = period,
    order          = ord,
    returned       = nrow(x),
    total_reported = if (is.null(attr(x, "total_results"))) NA_real_ else attr(x, "total_results"),
    duplicates     = sum(duplicated(x$video_id)),
    unique_videos  = n_distinct(x$video_id))) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(in_both = length(intersect(s$relevance$video_id, s$viewCount$video_id)))
}

top_channels <- function(s, period, n = 5) {
  imap(s, \(x, ord) x |>
         distinct(video_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
         count(channel_title, sort = TRUE, name = "videos") |>
         slice_head(n = n) |>
         mutate(period = period, order = ord, .before = 1)) |>
    list_rbind()
}

list_channel_videos() reads the channel’s uploads playlist, newest first, 50 videos per unit. Fetching one page at a time and stopping at the first page that crosses the start date counts exactly how many pages it took (ii below).

parse_uploads <- function(items) {
  tibble(
    video_id  = map_chr(items, \(i) pluck(i, "contentDetails", "videoId",
                  .default = pluck(i, "snippet", "resourceId", "videoId",
                                   .default = NA_character_))),
    published = map_chr(items, \(i) pluck(i, "contentDetails", "videoPublishedAt",
                  .default = pluck(i, "snippet", "publishedAt",
                                   .default = NA_character_))),
    title     = map_chr(items, \(i) pluck(i, "snippet", "title",
                                          .default = NA_character_))
  )
}

uploads_since <- function(channel_id, since, max_pages = 100) {
  pages <- list()
  token <- NULL
  repeat {
    resp <- list_channel_videos(channel_id, max_results = 50,
                                page_token = token, simplify = FALSE)
    page <- parse_uploads(resp$items)
    pages[[length(pages) + 1]] <- page
    token  <- resp$nextPageToken
    oldest <- suppressWarnings(min(as.Date(page$published), na.rm = TRUE))
    Sys.sleep(0.5)
    if (is.null(token) || oldest < since || length(pages) >= max_pages) break
  }
  videos <- list_rbind(pages) |> mutate(date = as.Date(published))
  list(videos = videos, pages = length(pages), oldest = min(videos$date, na.rm = TRUE))
}

  mutate(res    = map(channel_id, \(id) uploads_since(id, pre_since), .progress = TRUE),

         videos = map(res, "videos")) |>

route_summary <- function(uploads, route, search_ids, period) {
  uploads |>
    group_by(label, kind) |>
    summarise(uploads_in_window   = n(),
              kept_by_filter      = sum(match),
              kept_also_in_search = sum(match & video_id %in% search_ids),
              kept_not_in_search  = sum(match & !video_id %in% search_ids),
              in_search_but_dropped = sum(!match & video_id %in% search_ids),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    left_join(route |> select(label, pages, oldest), by = "label") |>
    mutate(period = period, .before = 1)
}

2d. Collect comments

d. Collect comments with collect_comments() (Part 5c) from two to four videos per channel, at most 300 comments per video. Write the collection log and the manifest (Part 5d). Record for each video the comment count it reports (get_video_stats()) and the number you received.

Statistics for the title-filtered uploads, then the n_videos_per_channel (3) most-viewed per channel. Videos with comments disabled are kept in the selection so the log records them; comment_count is missing when comments are disabled.

select_targets <- function(uploads, period) {
  kept <- uploads |> filter(match) |> distinct(video_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
  stats <- get_video_stats(kept$video_id) |>
    select(any_of(c("video_id", "view_count", "comment_count")))
  kept <- kept |> left_join(stats, by = "video_id", relationship = "one-to-one")

  status <- kept |>
    group_by(label) |>
    summarise(kept_videos = n(),
              comments_disabled_or_missing = sum(is.na(comment_count)),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(period = period, .before = 1)

  targets <- kept |>
    group_by(label) |>
    slice_max(view_count, n = n_videos_per_channel, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(period = period)

  list(targets = targets, status = status)
}

collect_comments() (Part 5c). Disabled comments and empty sections arrive as warnings (tuber_comments_disabled, tuber_no_comments) with an empty data frame; other failures are errors. Record each outcome and keep going.

collect_comments <- function(video_id, n_max = 300) {
  status <- "ok"
  out <- tryCatch(
    withCallingHandlers(
      get_all_comments(video_id, max_results = n_max),
      tuber_comments_disabled = function(w) {
        status <<- "disabled"; invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
      },
      tuber_no_comments = function(w) {
        if (status == "ok") status <<- "none"; invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
      }),
    error = function(e) e)
  # If tuber signals an empty section another way, still log it as "none"
  if (!inherits(out, "error") && status == "ok" && NROW(out) == 0) status <- "none"
  Sys.sleep(1)                                   # be polite
  if (inherits(out, "error")) {
    return(list(data = NULL,
                log  = tibble(video_id, status = "error", n = 0L,
                              message = conditionMessage(out))))
  }
  out <- as_tibble(out)
  if (nrow(out) > 0) out$video_id <- video_id   # replies can come back without it
  list(data = out,
       log  = tibble(video_id, status, n = nrow(out), message = NA_character_))
}


i. Before you join comments to video titles, make sure each video appears once and each comment once: distinct(comment_id, .keep_all = TRUE) and left_join(..., relationship = "many-to-one"). A repeated video otherwise copies its comments, and corpus() stops with docnames must be unique.

collect_set() keeps each video once and each comment once, then joins many-to-one. The log (Part 5d) records for each video reported (its comment_count from get_video_stats()) and received.

collect_set <- function(targets) {
  runs <- map(targets$video_id, collect_comments, n_max = n_comments_max,
              .progress = TRUE)
  video_meta <- targets |>
    distinct(video_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
    select(video_id, channel_title = label, video_title = title,
           video_date = date, period, view_count, reported = comment_count)

  log <- map(runs, "log") |>
    list_rbind() |>
    rename(received = n) |>
    mutate(collected_at = now_utc()) |>
    left_join(video_meta, by = "video_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
    relocate(channel_title, period, video_id, video_title, video_date,
             view_count, reported, received, status)

  comments <- map(runs, "data") |>
    list_rbind() |>
    distinct(comment_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
    left_join(video_meta |> select(video_id, channel_title, video_title, period),
              by = "video_id", relationship = "many-to-one")

  list(log = log, comments = comments)
}

ii. Check the manifest records the search term exactly as you sent it — and that the key is nowhere in it.

write_manifest() records how the data were collected and checks both before it returns.

write_manifest <- function(period, after, before, since, until,
                           searches, route_summary, targets, comments, path) {
  m <- list(
    source       = "YouTube Data API v3 via tuber",
    tuber        = as.character(packageVersion("tuber")),
    credential   = "API key (public data only); key not stored",
    period       = period,
    collected_at = now_utc(),
    search       = list(term             = search_term,
                        orders           = names(searches),
                        max_results      = n_search,
                        published_after  = after,
                        published_before = before,
                        returned         = map_int(searches, nrow),
                        total_reported   = map(searches, \(x) attr(x, "total_results")),
                        duplicates       = map_int(searches, \(x) sum(duplicated(x$video_id)))),
    channels     = route_summary |> select(label, kind, pages, oldest) |>
                     left_join(channels |> select(label, channel_id), by = "label"),
    channel_window = c(format(since), format(until)),
    title_filter = title_regex,
    selection    = sprintf(paste("Per channel, the %d most-viewed uploads in the window",
                                 "whose title matches the filter; at most %d comments",
                                 "(replies included) per video"),
                           n_videos_per_channel, n_comments_max),
    videos       = targets |> select(video_id, channel = label),
    n_videos     = nrow(targets),
    n_comments   = nrow(comments),
    retention    = "Delete or refresh within 30 days (YouTube API Developer Policies III.E.4.d)",
    delete_by    = format(Sys.Date() + 30)
  )
  write_json(m, path, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)

  # The term as sent, and no key anywhere in the file
  key <- Sys.getenv("YOUTUBE_KEY")
  stopifnot(identical(read_json(path)$search$term, search_term),
            !nzchar(key) || !any(grepl(key, readLines(path), fixed = TRUE)))
  invisible(m)
}

Important



The data expire. Comments collected with an API key are non-authorized data: the YouTube API Developer Policies (III.E.4.d) allow you to keep them for no more than 30 days. Write a delete_by date into each manifest, delete data/youtube/ by then, and make your report reproducible from the code and the manifest — not from a saved copy. Scraping YouTube pages or transcripts outside the API is not permitted (III.E.6); do not use yt-dlp or transcript scrapers for this assignment.




Rebuilding the comments from a manifest
After delete_by, the comments are gone; the published manifest and log are enough to collect them again. The manifest lists the videos and the search term; the log supplies each video’s title, date and reported count. A rebuild is a new collection: it starts a new 30-day clock, and it will not match the first one exactly, because comments are added and removed.

rebuild_from_manifest <- function(period_file) {        # "pre" or "post"
  m  <- read_json(file.path(dir_out, paste0("manifest_", period_file, ".json")),
                  simplifyVector = TRUE)
  lg <- read_csv(file.path(dir_out, paste0("log_", period_file, ".csv")),
                 show_col_types = FALSE)
  stopifnot(identical(m$search$term, search_term))

  targets <- as_tibble(m$videos) |>
    rename(label = channel) |>
    left_join(lg |> select(video_id, title = video_title, date = video_date,
                           view_count, comment_count = reported),
              by = "video_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
    mutate(period = m$period)

  coll <- collect_set(targets)
  write_rds(coll$comments, file.path(dir_yt, paste0("comments_", period_file, ".rds")))
  write_json(list(rebuilt_from = paste0("manifest_", period_file, ".json"),
                  collected_at = now_utc(),
                  n_videos     = nrow(targets),
                  n_comments   = nrow(coll$comments),
                  delete_by    = format(Sys.Date() + 30)),
             file.path(dir_out, paste0("rebuild_", period_file, ".json")),
             auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)
  coll
}

iv. How concentrated is authorship: what share of comments comes from the 10% most active authors? Exact duplicates? (Report counts, not names.)


share_top <- function(x, p) {
  x <- sort(x, decreasing = TRUE)
  k <- max(1, ceiling(p * length(x)))
  sum(x[seq_len(k)]) / sum(x)
}

describe_comments <- function(d) {
  per_author <- count(d, author_key)$n
  txt <- str_squish(str_to_lower(d$text_original))
  tibble(
    comments               = nrow(d),
    videos                 = n_distinct(d$video_id),
    reply_share            = mean(d$is_reply),
    likes_median           = median(d$like_count),
    likes_zero_share       = mean(d$like_count == 0),
    top1pct_like_share     = share_top(d$like_count, 0.01),
    authors                = length(per_author),
    top10pct_author_share  = share_top(per_author, 0.10),
    exact_duplicates       = sum(duplicated(txt)),
    written_after_election = mean(d$date > election_day),
    with_emoji             = mean(str_detect(d$text_original, "\\p{Extended_Pictographic}"))
  )
}

i. A corpus with docvars channel_title, video_id, is_reply, like_count, date, and a period (before / after Election Day). Say which unit you chose — comment or thread — and what you did with emoji, URLs and mentions.

The unit is the comment: each top-level comment and each reply is one document, with thread_id kept as a docvar so threads can be grouped later. URLs are removed (remove_url); emoji are removed with the other symbols (remove_symbols), so the dictionary below cannot see the tone they carry (their share is in 3a); @-mentions, which in replies name other commenters, are dropped as tokens.

corp_yt <- comments_all |>
  select(comment_id, text_original, channel_title, video_id, thread_id,
         is_reply, like_count, date, period) |>
  corpus(docid_field = "comment_id", text_field = "text_original")

summary(corp_yt, n = 5)

toks_base <- tokens(corp_yt, remove_punct = TRUE, remove_symbols = TRUE,
                    remove_url = TRUE, split_hyphens = TRUE) |>
  tokens_remove(pattern = "^@", valuetype = "regex") |>
  tokens_tolower()


ii. kwic() for democrat*, republican*, trump, vote*, ballot*. Read 20 lines for each before any model, and tally what the words are doing: naming a party, a candidate, the process, a grievance?

The sample goes to data/youtube/ (it contains comment text). Fill the use column with party, candidate, process, grievance or other, then tally.

kwic_patterns <- c("democrat*", "republican*", "trump", "vote*", "ballot*")
toks_read <- tokens(corp_yt)   # punctuation kept for reading

set.seed(6302)
kwic_read <- map(kwic_patterns, \(p) {
  k <- as.data.frame(kwic(toks_read, pattern = p, window = 8)) |> as_tibble()
  k |> slice_sample(n = min(20, nrow(k))) |> mutate(pattern = p, hits = nrow(k))
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(use = NA_character_)

write_csv(kwic_read, file.path(dir_yt, "kwic_reading.csv"))


kwic_coded <- read_csv(file.path(dir_yt, "kwic_reading.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
kwic_tally <- kwic_coded |>
  count(pattern, hits, use) |>
  group_by(pattern) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()
kwic_tally
write_csv(kwic_tally, file.path(dir_out, "kwic_tally.csv"))

v. Sentiment by channel and period with data_dictionary_LSD2015 and dfm_lookup(). Validate it: hand-code 40 randomly sampled comments as positive, negative or neither, and report agreement with the dictionary. Where does a dictionary misread election talk (sarcasm, “landslide”, “rigged”)?

The Lexicoder Sentiment Dictionary. dfm_lookup() works on single words, so the dictionary’s negated-phrase keys (neg_positive, neg_negative) are left out; negation is not handled.

lsd     <- data_dictionary_LSD2015[c("negative", "positive")]
dfm_lsd <- dfm(toks_base) |> dfm_lookup(dictionary = lsd)

  as_tibble() |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(docvars(dfm_lsd))) |>
  mutate(dict = case_when(positive > negative ~ "positive",
                          negative > positive ~ "negative",
                          TRUE                ~ "neither"))

sent_group <- sent_doc |>
  group_by(channel_title, period) |>
  summarise(comments  = n(),
            positive  = sum(positive),
            negative  = sum(negative),
            net_tone  = (positive - negative) / (positive + negative),
            share_pos = mean(dict == "positive"),
            share_neg = mean(dict == "negative"),
            .groups = "drop")
sent_group
write_csv(sent_group, file.path(dir_out, "sentiment_by_channel_period.csv"))

p_sent <- ggplot(sent_group, aes(channel_title, net_tone, fill = period)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "net tone (pos - neg) / (pos + neg)")

Validation: 40 comments drawn at random and coded by hand as positive, negative or neither — blind: the coding sheet has no dictionary column.

  left_join(comments_all |> select(doc_id = comment_id, text_original), by = "doc_id")

  left_join(read_rds(file.path(dir_yt, "handcode_dict.rds")), by = "doc_id")

p_o   <- mean(coded$hand == coded$dict)
lvls  <- c("positive", "negative", "neither")
p_e   <- sum(sapply(lvls, \(k) mean(coded$hand == k) * mean(coded$dict == k)))
kappa <- (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)

write_csv(tibble(n = nrow(coded), agreement = p_o, cohen_kappa = kappa),
          file.path(dir_out, "sentiment_validation.csv"))
write_csv(count(coded, hand, dict), file.path(dir_out, "sentiment_confusion.csv"))

c. Compare with Assignment 6. Biden–Xi 2021 tweets; presidential documents mentioning Xi; midterm 2026 comments. For each: who produced the text, for whom, what selected it, whether it can be collected again, and what kind of claim it can support — about the public, an audience, or a government.

Presidential documents mentioning Xi (CPD)
Midterm 2026 YouTube comments




Who produced the text
Twitter users posting during the November 2021 video summit
The White House; compiled by the Office of the Federal Register
Viewers who chose to comment under these videos


For whom
Followers and the platform’s public
The public record
Other viewers of the video and the channel


What selected it
A keyword and a collection window; what the API returned then

About the commenting audience of these videos, as YouTube showed it




i. Optional. Reply network with vosonSML (Part 9): who replies to whom, and is the conversation one crowd or several?

Same key, same quota; report network size only.

# install.packages(c("vosonSML", "igraph"))
library(vosonSML)
ok_videos <- coll_pre$log |> filter(status == "ok") |> pull(video_id)
yt_auth   <- Authenticate("youtube", apiKey = Sys.getenv("YOUTUBE_KEY"))
yt_data   <- Collect(yt_auth, videoIDs = ok_videos[1:3], maxComments = 300,
                     writeToFile = FALSE, verbose = TRUE)
actor_net <- Create(yt_data, "actor") |> Graph()
igraph::vcount(actor_net); igraph::ecount(actor_net)
igraph::components(actor_net)$no   # one crowd or several?


ii. Optional. Rerun one comment request with httr2 (Part 8) and confirm you get the same first page. What does tuber add?

tuber builds this request with the key in a redacted x-goog-api-key header.

library(httr2)
ok_videos <- coll_pre$log |> filter(status == "ok") |> pull(video_id)
one_vid   <- ok_videos[1]

req <- request("https://www.googleapis.com/youtube/v3/commentThreads") |>
  req_url_query(part = "snippet", videoId = one_vid, maxResults = 100,
                textFormat = "plainText") |>
  req_headers_redacted("x-goog-api-key" = Sys.getenv("YOUTUBE_KEY"))
req                        # the key prints as <REDACTED>

resp     <- req |> req_perform() |> resp_body_json()
ids_raw  <- map_chr(resp$items, "id")
ids_tub  <- list_comment_threads(video_id = one_vid, text_format = "plainText",
                                 max_results = 100)
setequal(ids_raw, ids_tub[[intersect(c("id", "comment_id", "thread_id"),
                                     names(ids_tub))[1]]])







Note



Every comment section has a data-generating process. Who chose to comment, under which video, on which channel; what the channel moderated and YouTube held back; how order ranked what you saw first; when you ran the query — before or after the result was known. In an election season, add who comments many times and what repeated text may be. Say which in your report — it decides whether your keyness and sentiment results describe voters, an audience, or the comments YouTube showed you.

title: EPPS 6302 Methods of Data Collection and Production: Assignment 7
text:
4. Submit

a. Post assign07.qmd under Assignments on your website, with the plots, the quota table, a short report (about 700 words), and the data note for the YouTube collection: source; permission (API terms, key, quota, 30-day retention); method (search term, windows, order, channels, title filter, caps); selection; known gaps.
b. Post the collection logs, the manifests and aggregate tables only — not the comments, not author names or channel IDs of commenters, and not your key. Quote at most a few short comments, without their authors, and do not quote claims about voting or fraud without saying what they are.

The resources: lines in the YAML copy every CSV and JSON in results/assign07/ to the site with the page; nothing in data/youtube/ is copied. Run this before rendering for the site: it stops if the key, or a column holding comment text or commenter names or channel IDs, is in any published file.

key   <- Sys.getenv("YOUTUBE_KEY")
files <- list.files(dir_out, pattern = "\\.(csv|json)$", full.names = TRUE)

has_key <- files |>
  keep(\(f) nzchar(key) && any(grepl(key, readLines(f, warn = FALSE), fixed = TRUE)))

blocked  <- c("text_original", "text_display", "author_name", "author_display_name",
              "author_channel_id", "author_channel_url", "author_profile_image_url")
has_cols <- files[str_detect(files, "\\.csv$")] |>
  keep(\(f) any(names(read_csv(f, n_max = 0, show_col_types = FALSE)) %in% blocked))

stopifnot("key found in a published file" = length(has_key) == 0,
          "commenter fields found in a published table" = length(has_cols) == 0)
basename(files)                               # what will be posted


Report
The collection. I searched “US midterm election” twice per period. Before Election Day (videos published 1 September – 27 October), each ordering returned 100 results against a reported 1,000,000, which is YouTube’s capped estimate, not a count. Only 17 videos appeared in both lists. Al Jazeera English led the relevance ordering (38 of 99 unique videos) and CNN the view-count ordering (37 of 100). After Election Day the overlap was 23, with 5 and 6 duplicates. None of my three channels led either list, so I reached their videos through their uploads.
The channel route found what search missed. Before Election Day, BBC News, Fox News and NBC News uploaded 1,271, 3,022 and 2,889 videos; the title filter kept 410, and only 3 of those appeared in either search. Reaching 1 September took 32, 75 and 72 pages: 179 units against the 55 I planned, because these channels post 22 to 53 videos a day, not 10 to 20. The whole collection used 390 units and 8 search calls, against a plan of 258 and 8. The filter was too broad: election and vote let in foreign elections and a UN vote, so three of the nine pre-election videos are about Israel, Serbia and a world map. All nine post-election titles concern the midterms.
What came back. Each of the 18 videos returned exactly 300 comments while reporting between 311 and 6,335, so the cap accounts for nearly the whole gap; comments held for review or deleted cannot be told apart from it. All 18 requests succeeded; among the candidate videos, BBC had two with comments disabled. Replies are 13% of comments (2 to 146 per video). Likes are concentrated: 70% of comments have none, and the top 1% hold 53% of all likes. Authorship is less so: 4,609 authors wrote 5,400 comments, and the most active 10% wrote 23%. There are 61 exact duplicates. Fewer than 2% of the pre-election comments were written after Election Day, although I collected them six days later.
Reading and counting. trump (920 hits) and vote* (682) outnumber democrat* (489), republican* (334) and ballot* (72). [Tally from the kwic() reading: the share of the 20 lines per word that name a party, a candidate, the process or a grievance.] The sheet’s phrases are rare in 5,400 comments: senate race 8 times, early voting 5, mail in 5, election fraud 3, house majority none. [My two phrases and their counts.]
[Keyness: what distinguishes each channel’s comments, and after from before; whether it is about the election or the audience.]
By the Lexicoder dictionary, Fox News comments are the most negative before the election (net tone −0.26) and less so after (−0.17); NBC News comments move from neutral (0.04) to positive (0.24); BBC News comments move from neutral (−0.04) to negative (−0.15). [Hand-coding: agreement and kappa on 40 comments.] The dictionary misreads election talk. It has no entry for landslide or rigged, so “Yeah…. I’m sure this election wasn’t rigged”, a sarcastic, unsupported claim of fraud, scores as neutral. It scores flip, which in election talk usually means a seat changing party, as negative, and win as positive whichever side wins.
Three corpora. The Biden–Xi tweets were written by users for their followers, selected by keyword and window, and cannot be collected again; they support a claim about an online audience at one moment. The presidential documents were written by the White House for the record, selected by editorial inclusion and my query, and can be retrieved again; they support a claim about what a government said. The comments were written by viewers for other viewers, selected by my channels, filter, view counts and cap, and can only partly be collected again; they support a claim about the commenting audience of these videos.
The data-generating process. Viewers chose to comment. I chose three channels, a title filter that let in off-topic videos, and the most-viewed matches. The channels decided where comments were open, and YouTube ordered each section, so the cap kept the first 300 of up to 6,335. A few comments hold most of the likes, though no small group of authors dominates. The post-election sections were still filling when I collected them. The keyness and sentiment results therefore describe neither voters nor these channels’ audiences, but the comments YouTube showed me on 18 videos on 9 November 2026.


Data note
Source. Public YouTube video metadata and comments (with replies), from the YouTube Data API v3 through the tuber package (3.0.0).
Permission. Collected with an API key only, under the YouTube API Services Terms and Developer Policies, within the default daily quota (search calls and units budgeted in 2a). Comments collected with an API key are non-authorized data and may be kept no more than 30 days (Developer Policies III.E.4.d): the raw comments in data/youtube/ are excluded from the public repository and must be deleted by 2026-12-09 (pre-election collection) and 2026-12-09 (post-election collection). The report is reproducible from the code and the manifests (see Rebuilding the comments from a manifest), not from a saved copy. No YouTube pages or transcripts were scraped outside the API (III.E.6). This page publishes code, logs, manifests and aggregate tables only: log before, log after, manifest before, manifest after, and the other tables in results/assign07/.
Method. Search term “US midterm election”, ordered by relevance and by view count, 100 results each, for videos published 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z to 2026-10-28T00:00:00Z (exclusive) and 2026-11-04T00:00:00Z to 2026-11-09T19:35:27Z. Channels: NBC News (national network), Fox News (cable news), BBC News (international broadcaster), listed through their uploads playlists and filtered by title with the pattern midterm|election|senate|house race|ballot|\bvot(e|es|er|ers|ing)\b|congress. From each channel the 3 most-viewed matching videos per period, at most 300 comments each. Collected 2026-11-09 19:30:00 UTC and 2026-11-09 19:36:14 UTC.
Selection. These are the publicly visible comments, at the time of collection, on the most-viewed election-titled videos of three chosen channels. They are not a sample of public opinion, of YouTube viewers, or of all midterm videos. Search returns a ranking, not a sample; the title filter decides which uploads count as election coverage; taking the most-viewed videos favors the largest audiences; the cap keeps the comments YouTube ranks first and drops the tail; removed or held comments never appear, and videos with comments disabled contribute nothing.
Known gaps. Viewers who watch without commenting, people not on YouTube, and anyone whose comment was held or removed. Comments carry no location, so commenters cannot be tied to a state or district. A few authors may write a large share of the comments (3a). Comments keep arriving and some are deleted, so a re-collection will not match; post-election comment sections were collected while still filling.

References

2. Look at what you got

a. What range of dates does the file cover?
2021-09-01 to 2026-09-01


b. Interval
What is the interval — hourly, daily, weekly, monthly? Now change the date window and download again csv. Did the interval change?
The five-year dataset uses monthly observations. After changing the window to “Last 24 hours,” the interval changed to 16 minutes because Google Trends automatically adjusts its temporal resolution to the selected time window.


c. What are the units? What does a value of 100 mean, and 0?
These are a normalized search-interest index from 0–100, based on the proportion of searches for the term relative to all searches in the selected place and time period.

100 = the point of peak relative search interest within the selected dataset.
50 = relative search interest was half the peak level.
0 = insufficient search volume to report a value; it does not necessarily mean zero searches occurred.



d. Now remove one search term and download again.
Did the numbers for the remaining terms stay the same?
Dropped Trump from the Past 5 years search. The values for Kamala Harris and Election stayed exactly the same across all 61 monthly observations. Removing Trump did not alter the scale in this comparison because Election still supplied the peak value of 100, while Trump had a maximum value of 40. csv

title: Assignment 02
text:
3. Collect it from R

a. gtrends package
Use the gtrendsR package and the gtrendsR01.R program. The first call in that script is the same query you just ran by hand:

library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)

# Store successful Google Trends downloads here.
cache_dir <- "_gtrends_cache"
dir.create(cache_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Download each query only once. If Google temporarily blocks the request,
# retry with exponential backoff until a successful result is returned.
# Once saved as an RDS file, future renders read the local file and never
# contact Google Trends for that query again.
cached_gtrends <- function(cache_name, ..., initial_wait = 60, max_wait = 600) {
  cache_file <- file.path(cache_dir, cache_name)

  if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
    return(readRDS(cache_file))
  }

  attempt <- 1L

  repeat {
    result <- tryCatch(
      gtrends(...),
      error = function(e) {
        message(
          "Google Trends request failed on attempt ", attempt,
          ": ", conditionMessage(e)
        )
        NULL
      }
    )

    if (!is.null(result)) {
      saveRDS(result, cache_file)
      message("Google Trends data saved to: ", cache_file)
      return(result)
    }

    wait <- min(initial_wait * 2^(attempt - 1L), max_wait)
    wait <- wait + runif(1, 0, 15)
    message("Retrying in ", round(wait), " seconds...")
    Sys.sleep(wait)
    attempt <- attempt + 1L
  }
}

TrumpHarrisElection <- cached_gtrends(
  "trump_harris_election_us_5y.rds",
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

the_df <- TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time
plot(TrumpHarrisElection)

}

c. Section 6 of the script runs names(tct).
That call left onlyInterest at its default, so the object carries several data frames. Which of them did the website CSV not give you?
With onlyInterest left at its default, names(tct) returns:

names(tct)

[1] "interest_over_time"  "interest_by_country" "interest_by_region" 
[4] "interest_by_dma"     "interest_by_city"    "related_topics"     
[7] "related_queries"    


The additional data frames that the website CSV did not provide were:

interest_by_country — search interest summarized by country.
interest_by_region — search interest summarized by region or subregion.
interest_by_dma — search interest by designated market area (media market).
interest_by_city — search interest summarized by city.
related_topics — topics associated with the search term.
related_queries — other search queries associated with the term.

A note on terms The website instructions above say Kamala Harris. The script searches Harris.

a. Pull both and compare the series. Are they the same?

harris_compare <- cached_gtrends(
  "harris_vs_kamala_harris_us_5y.rds",
  c("Harris", "Kamala Harris"),
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0,
  onlyInterest = TRUE
)

harris_plot <- plot(harris_compare)

harris_plot +
  ggplot2::theme(
    plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(t = 16, r = 8, b = 8, l = 8)
  )




Weekly relative search interest for Harris and Kamala Harris in the United States, September 2021–September 2026.





harris_numeric <- harris_compare$interest_over_time |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    hits_numeric = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(hits))),
    hits_numeric = dplyr::if_else(
      as.character(hits) == "<1",
      0.5,
      hits_numeric
    )
  )

harris_means <- harris_numeric |>
  dplyr::group_by(keyword) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    observations = dplyr::n(),
    mean_interest = mean(hits_numeric),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

harris_by_date <- harris_numeric |>
  dplyr::filter(keyword == "Harris") |>
  dplyr::select(date, harris = hits_numeric) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    harris_numeric |>
      dplyr::filter(keyword == "Kamala Harris") |>
      dplyr::select(date, kamala_harris = hits_numeric),
    by = "date"
  )

harris_gap <- harris_by_date |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    matched_dates = dplyr::n(),
    dates_harris_higher = sum(harris > kamala_harris),
    mean_gap = mean(harris - kamala_harris)
  )

harris_means

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  keyword       observations mean_interest
  <chr>                <int>         <dbl>
1 Harris                 262          9.19
2 Kamala Harris          262          2.02

harris_gap

  matched_dates dates_harris_higher mean_gap
1           262                 262 7.171756


The Harris and Kamala Harris series are not the same. Across 262 weekly observations, the mean Google Trends index was 9.19 for Harris and 2.02 for Kamala Harris, an average gap of 7.17 points. Harris had the higher value on all 262 dates. These normalized values show relative interest within this joint comparison; they are not raw search counts.


b. Harris
Harris is also a county, a supermarket chain, and several thousand other people. What does that gap tell you about the difference between a search term and the concept you meant to measure?
This gap shows that a search term is not necessarily identical to the concept being measured. Harris is an ambiguous term that can capture searches concerning Kamala Harris as well as unrelated people, places, and organizations. The results do not reveal how much of the broader Harris series actually concerns Kamala Harris. Therefore, using Harris to measure interest in Kamala Harris introduces measurement error, while the more specific Kamala Harris query better represents the intended concept.

title: Assignment 02
text:
4. Compare the two methods

a. Line the two series up. Are the numbers identical? If not, by how much, and in which direction?
The website query used Kamala Harris, while the R script used Harris. To avoid treating those different search terms as equivalent, this comparison uses the two terms shared by both pulls: Trump and Election. The website data are monthly, whereas the R data are weekly, so the R observations are averaged by month and rescaled to a 0–100 index. The incomplete first and last months are excluded, leaving 59 complete months for each term.

website_common <- read_csv(
  "time_series_US_20210912-0854_20260912-0854.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  dplyr::select(date = Time, Trump, Election) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "keyword",
    values_to = "website_hits"
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    date >= as.Date("2021-10-01"),
    date <= as.Date("2026-08-01")
  )

r_monthly <- the_df |>
  dplyr::filter(keyword %in% c("Trump", "election")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    keyword = dplyr::recode(keyword, election = "Election"),
    r_hits = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(hits))),
    r_hits = dplyr::if_else(as.character(hits) == "<1", 0.5, r_hits),
    date = as.Date(date),
    month = as.Date(format(date, "%Y-%m-01"))
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(month, keyword) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    r_monthly_mean = mean(r_hits),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    month >= as.Date("2021-10-01"),
    month <= as.Date("2026-08-01")
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    r_monthly_index = 100 * r_monthly_mean / max(r_monthly_mean)
  )

method_comparison <- website_common |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    r_monthly,
    by = c("date" = "month", "keyword")
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    difference = r_monthly_index - website_hits,
    absolute_difference = abs(difference)
  )

method_comparison_by_term <- method_comparison |>
  dplyr::group_by(keyword) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    months = dplyr::n(),
    mean_website = mean(website_hits),
    mean_r = mean(r_monthly_index),
    mean_difference = mean(difference),
    mean_absolute_difference = mean(absolute_difference),
    maximum_absolute_difference = max(absolute_difference),
    correlation = cor(website_hits, r_monthly_index),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

method_comparison_overall <- method_comparison |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    observations_compared = dplyr::n(),
    observations_different = sum(abs(difference) > 1e-9),
    mean_difference = mean(difference),
    mean_absolute_difference = mean(absolute_difference),
    maximum_absolute_difference = max(absolute_difference)
  )

election_comparison <- method_comparison_by_term |>
  dplyr::filter(keyword == "Election")

trump_comparison <- method_comparison_by_term |>
  dplyr::filter(keyword == "Trump")

method_comparison_by_term

  keyword  months mean_website mean_r mean_difference mean_absolute_difference
  <chr>     <int>        <dbl>  <dbl>           <dbl>                    <dbl>
1 Election     59         4.68   5.20           0.518                    0.900
2 Trump        59        10.7   10.3           -0.401                    0.719

method_comparison_overall

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  observations_compared observations_different mean_difference
                  <int>                  <int>           <dbl>
1                   118                    117          0.0584
# ℹ 2 more variables: mean_absolute_difference <dbl>,
#   maximum_absolute_difference <dbl>

method_comparison |>
  dplyr::select(date, keyword, Website = website_hits, R = r_monthly_index) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Website, R),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "interest"
  ) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(x = date, y = interest, color = method)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~keyword, ncol = 1) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Date",
    y = "Relative search interest",
    color = "Source"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()




Monthly Google Trends indices from the website and R for the two shared search terms, October 2021–August 2026.




The numbers are not identical: 117 of 118 matched term-month observations differed. Across both terms, the mean absolute difference was 0.81 points and the maximum absolute difference was 4.61 points. On average, the R index for Election was 0.52 points higher than the website index, while the R index for Trump was 0.4 points lower. Despite the small numerical differences, the series have very similar shapes: their correlations are 0.997 for Election and 0.994 for Trump. This remains an approximate comparison because the original queries used different Harris terms and Google Trends relies on sampled, normalized data.


b. What are the differences between the two methods? Consider at least:

i. Reproducibility — could someone else regenerate your file exactly?
Neither method guarantees that another person can reproduce the exact values by making a new request, because Google Trends draws from sampled data and a moving “last five years” window. The R method makes the procedure more reproducible because the code records the query and analysis steps. Exact numerical reproduction depends on retaining and sharing the cached raw data used for the analysis.


ii. Provenance — which method records the query parameters for you?
The R method provides stronger provenance because the function call explicitly records the search terms, geography, time window, category, and search type. The website download requires those selections and the pull time to be documented manually in a datasheet; the CSV alone does not preserve the complete collection procedure.


iii. Scale — what happens when you need fifty terms instead of three?
Collecting fifty terms manually would require many repeated website searches and downloads, increasing both labor and the risk of inconsistent settings. R can automate the repeated calls, file naming, validation, and caching. However, the terms must still be divided into batches because the service limits comparisons, and the batches need a shared anchor term if their separately normalized indices are to be placed on a common scale.


iv. Fragility — what breaks, and how would you know?
The website method is vulnerable to interface changes, inconsistent manual selections, and misplaced downloads. The R method depends on gtrendsR and an unofficial endpoint, so changes to the service can break requests or parsing; rate limiting can also return errors such as HTTP 429. Failures should be detected by checking request errors, expected columns, date ranges, row counts, missing values, and the 0–100 range before analysis. Caching the first successful pull prevents later endpoint failures from changing an already completed analysis.



c. Run section 7 of the script: the same call twice, a few minutes apart.
Do you get the same numbers?

# These use two different cache files intentionally so the assignment captures
# two Google Trends samples collected three minutes apart. Each sample is
# downloaded only once.
first_cache_name <- "repeat_trump_harris_election_spaced_1.rds"
second_cache_name <- "repeat_trump_harris_election_spaced_2.rds"

repeat_pull_1 <- cached_gtrends(
  first_cache_name,
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

# Wait only when the second sample has not yet been cached. Later renders reuse
# both files without waiting or contacting Google Trends again.
second_cache_file <- file.path(cache_dir, second_cache_name)

if (!file.exists(second_cache_file)) {
  message("Waiting three minutes before the second pull...")
  Sys.sleep(180)
}

repeat_pull_2 <- cached_gtrends(
  second_cache_name,
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

repeat_pull_times <- data.frame(
  pull = c("Pull 1", "Pull 2"),
  cached_at = file.info(
    file.path(
      cache_dir,
      c(first_cache_name, second_cache_name)
    )
  )$mtime
)

repeat_pull_times

    pull           cached_at
1 Pull 1 2026-09-15 09:12:36
2 Pull 2 2026-09-15 09:15:37

pull_1 <- repeat_pull_1$interest_over_time
pull_2 <- repeat_pull_2$interest_over_time

# Convert Google Trends scores to numbers.
# "<1" is represented by its midpoint, 0.5.
hits_to_numeric <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  result <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  result[x == "<1"] <- 0.5
  result
}

pull_comparison <- pull_1 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    date,
    keyword,
    hits_1_raw = hits,
    hits_1 = hits_to_numeric(hits)
  ) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    pull_2 |>
      dplyr::transmute(
        date,
        keyword,
        hits_2_raw = hits,
        hits_2 = hits_to_numeric(hits)
      ),
    by = c("date", "keyword")
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    difference = hits_2 - hits_1,
    absolute_difference = abs(difference)
  )

pull_summary <- pull_comparison |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    exactly_identical = all(hits_1_raw == hits_2_raw),
    observations_compared = dplyr::n(),
    observations_different = sum(hits_1_raw != hits_2_raw),
    mean_absolute_difference = mean(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum_absolute_difference = max(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

pull_summary

  exactly_identical observations_compared observations_different
1             FALSE                   786                     15
  mean_absolute_difference maximum_absolute_difference
1                0.0178117                           1


The two pulls did not return exactly the same values. Of the 786 matched observations, 15 differed. The mean absolute difference was 0.02 points, and the maximum absolute difference was 1 point.
The first pull was cached at 2026-09-15 09:12:36 CDT, and the second was cached at 2026-09-15 09:15:37 CDT.
What does your answer imply about every finding you might report from this source?
Because Google Trends uses sampled and normalized search data, its values should be interpreted as estimates rather than exact counts. Repeated pulls may produce slightly different values, although the broad pattern may remain stable. Each successful pull should therefore be cached, documented, and interpreted without overemphasizing small numerical differences.

text:
Are small data methods still needed in the big data age? Why, and how?

Big data does not eliminate the need for systematic small data methodologies. In fact, it could be argued that it increases the need for the need for these methodologies. It is very important to understand the data generating process, as well as the context, representativeness, etc. of the sample itself. More is not better, just more. Without understanding these processes, the inference from the sample set is limited.

title: EPPS 6302 Methods of Data Collection and Production: Prepare for Class 7
section: 4. Prepare answers — analytics of text data
text:
4. Prepare answers — analytics of text data

How are text data generated? Who wrote the text, for whom, and what decided which texts you can collect?

In general text is generated by people writing, although that will be changing in the future. The content reflects an author’s purpose, intended audience, and the context for which it was produced.
What texts can be collected are determined by social, legal and mechanical constraints. Social is defined by our morals and ethics. Legal is defined by our laws. Mechanical is defined by what is actually available.

What is a topic, and what would convince you a topic model found one?

A topic is a common theme or subject found across documents. Topic models identify groups of words that often appear together, helping researchers find themes in large collections of text.
To decide whether a model found meaningful topics, I would look at the words associated with each topic and read some of the documents individually. The topics should make sense, be different from one another, and appear consistently when the model is run again. I would also compare the results with human analysis.
For our data center research, topics might include electricity use, water consumption, economic development, and local opposition. A good model would identify these themes and connect them to documents that actually discuss those issues.

What does a sentiment score measure — and what does a dictionary miss?

A sentiment score measures how positive or negative a text is. Dictionary-based methods assign values to words and combine them to estimate the overall tone of a document. Some methods also measure emotions such as fear, anger, etc.
Dictionary methods have limitations because they often miss context, sarcasm, and how words are used. For example, the word “power” might be positive in one context but neutral when discussing electricity.
For our data center research, sentiment scores could help show differences in how data centers are discussed. However, a positive or negative score does not necessarily mean the author supports or opposes data centers. It could just be based on quotes. Comparing the scores with documents reviewed by people would help determine how accurate the results are.

How would you place a text on a position or polarity scale, and against what would you validate it?

A text can be placed on a scale using dictionaries, classification models, or statistical methods such as Wordfish. These methods estimate where a document falls between two positions, such as supporting or opposing a policy.
For our data center research, I would use a scale ranging from opposition to support. A model could be trained using documents that people have already classified, with neutral or mixed positions placed near the middle.
To check the results, I would compare the model’s scores with documents independently reviewed by people. I would also check whether different reviewers agree and whether the model produces consistent results across sources. This is important because a document might discuss negative environmental effects while still supporting data center development.

title: EPPS 6302 Methods of Data Collection and Production: Prepare for Class 10
text:
5. Discuss — linkage methods and algorithms

Linkage methods.

Deterministic linkage. Two records match when chosen fields agree exactly, or agree under a fixed rule. What does a typo, a married name, or a missing birth date do to that rule? Who is most likely to be missed?


A fixed rule leaves no room for error, so one bad field breaks the match. A typo or nickname drops a true pair below the cutoff. A married name splits one woman into two records, and if surname is a blocking key the pair is never compared at all. A missing birth date leaves the rule nothing to evaluate. Rules also give no threshold for trading false matches against missed ones, and loosening them adds false matches among common names. The people missed are those with messy or changing records: women who changed surnames, people with hyphenated or transliterated names (Tokle and Bender note Asian names were harder to match uniquely), frequent movers, and anyone with incomplete records. Because these misses cluster by sex, ethnicity and class, the linked file is a selected sample.
ii. *Probabilistic linkage.* Each pair of records gets a probability of being a match, from how often fields agree among true matches and among non-matches. Where does that probability come from when no one has labelled the true matches?
In the Fellegi–Sunter model, each field comparison has an m-probability (agreement among true matches) and a u-probability (agreement among non-matches), and their ratio is the match weight. With no labelled matches, match status is treated as a latent class, and the probabilities are estimated by EM from the comparison patterns themselves. fastLink does this and treats missing values as missing at random (Enamorado et al., 2019). The probability is therefore only as good as the model’s assumptions of conditionally independent fields and ignorable missingness. Turning probabilities into links requires a threshold, often with a clerical-review band. Raising it trades false matches for missed ones, so the linkage should be validated against a hand-reviewed sample.
iii. *Statistical matching vs. exact matching.* Exact matching looks for the same person or unit in two files. Statistical matching combines files that share no units, by pairing similar units. What can each support you in claiming — about individuals, and about populations?
Exact matching finds the same unit in both files. It supports individual-level claims and population-level claims about joint distributions, subject to linkage error. Statistical matching pairs similar but different units, so it produces a synthetic file. It supports no claims about individuals, and only population claims that rest on an untestable assumption: the variables unique to each file are conditionally independent given the matching variables. When that fails, relationships across the two files are biased toward zero.

Linkage algorithms. Trace one pair of records through the steps of ch. 3: preprocessing (standardizing names, dates, addresses), blocking, comparison (exact, or string distance such as Jaro–Winkler), classification by threshold, and enforcing one-to-one links. Which step do you think does most to decide the result? Which is least reported?

Tracing one pair. Take two records for the same woman. In a voter file she is “MARIA GARCIA-LOPEZ, 07/03/1985, 12 Elm Street, Apt 4.” In a later administrative file she is “Maria Lopez, 1985-03-07, 12 Elm St #4.”
Preprocessing standardizes both records: case, punctuation, and address abbreviations (“Street” to “St”, “Apt 4” and “#4” to a common unit field), with names parsed into first, last and middle. It also has to resolve the date. Read “07/03/1985” as US month/day, and it becomes July 3, which no longer matches the March 7 in the second file. Read it as day/month, and it agrees. Nothing in the data settles that; a coding choice does.
Blocking then decides whether the pair is ever compared. If the block is last name plus birth year, the records land in different blocks (“GARCIA-LOPEZ” vs. “LOPEZ”), and the true match is lost before any scoring happens. Blocking on birth year plus ZIP code keeps them together.
Comparison scores each field. First name agrees exactly. Last name gets a partial Jaro–Winkler score, because “LOPEZ” is only part of “GARCIA-LOPEZ”. Date and address agree after standardization.
Classification sums these into a match weight and compares it with a threshold. A clean surname agreement would have cleared it easily; the partial surname score may leave the pair in the clerical-review band.
One-to-one enforcement finally resolves conflicts. If another “Maria Lopez” in the same block scores slightly higher, the Hungarian assignment can give her this record, and our true pair loses even after passing the threshold.
Which step does most to decide the result.
Blocking. Every other step can be revisited: a pair scored badly can be rescored, and a threshold can be moved. But a pair that blocking separates is never compared, so no later step can recover it. Its failures are also systematic. Blocking on surname drops exactly the people whose names changed, and the chapter flags name changes and moves as the cases exact blocking keys miss. Preprocessing comes close, since it determines what the blocking keys contain.
Which is least reported.
Preprocessing. Papers usually report the blocking scheme, the comparison functions and the threshold, but rarely the standardization rules: which nicknames were mapped, how hyphenated and compound surnames were split, which date format was assumed, how addresses were parsed. These choices often live in undocumented cleaning scripts. Yet they set the inputs to every later step, and they fall unevenly on people with non-Anglo names, compound surnames or nonstandard addresses. Blocking is a close second: studies often say what they blocked on but almost never estimate how many true matches the blocking excluded.






A linked file is produced, not found. Linkage creates records that existed in neither source. Its errors are false matches and missed matches — and they are not random: they fall harder on people with common names, changed names, or incomplete records. Come ready to say how you would report a linkage, and how you would know it worked.



Bring: the readings annotated, fastLink installed, notes from the colloquium talk if you attended, and one dataset from your team project you might link to another — with the fields you would link on.

make_data() also records what the generator did to each true match, by comparing the copied fields. This is known only because the data are simulated; it is used to name error causes in 4a.

std_records <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    mutate(
      first_name_std = ws$standardize_names(first_name),
      last_name_std  = ws$standardize_names(last_name),
      first_initial  = substr(first_name_std, 1, 1),
      dob_std        = ws$standardize_date(dob)
    )
}

make_data <- function(corruption_rate = 0.20, n = 500, num_matches = 100) {
  set.seed(42)   # keep: the seed stays at the top of the data generator
  trs <- ws$create_trs_data(n)
  tea <- ws$create_tea_data(trs, n, num_matches, corruption_rate)
  key <- ws$create_validation_set(trs, tea, num_matches)

  # What the generator did to each true match (one change at most per record)
  i <- seq_len(num_matches)
  dgp <- tibble(
    trs_record_id = trs$record_id[i],
    tea_record_id = tea$record_id[i],
    first_changed = trs$first_name[i] != tea$first_name[i],
    last_changed  = trs$last_name[i]  != tea$last_name[i],
    dob_changed   = trs$dob[i]        != tea$dob[i],
    last_std_same = ws$standardize_names(trs$last_name[i]) ==
                    ws$standardize_names(tea$last_name[i]),
    corruption = case_when(
      first_changed                ~ "Abbreviation",
      last_changed & last_std_same ~ "Typo erased by standardizing",
      last_changed                 ~ "Typo",
      dob_changed                  ~ "Date corruption",
      TRUE                         ~ "None"
    )
  )
  list(rate = corruption_rate, trs = std_records(trs), tea = std_records(tea),
       key = key, dgp = dgp)
}

title: EPPS 6302 Methods of Data Collection and Production: Assignment 8
text:
1. Read

a. Foster, Ian, Rayid Ghani, Ron S. Jarmin, Frauke Kreuter, and Julia Lane, eds. 2020. Big Data and Social Science, Chapter 3, https://textbook.coleridgeinitiative.org/chap-link.html.
b. Enamorado, Ted, Benjamin Fifield, and Kosuke Imai. 2019. “Using a Probabilistic Model to Assist Merging of Large-scale Administrative Records.” American Political Science Review 113 (2): 353–371. Read Sections 1–2 and the discussion of the model’s assumptions.
c. Answer in two sentences each: what does the Fellegi-Sunter model estimate that the workshop’s weighted score does not? Why does the paper treat records with a unique ID differently from records without one?

What Fellegi-Sunter estimates. The model treats match status as a hidden variable and estimates, for each field, how often true matches agree (m) and how often non-matches agree (u), together with the share of pairs that are matches; from these it gives each pair a probability of being a match and, for any threshold, the expected false discovery and false negative rates (Enamorado et al., 2019; Fellegi & Sunter, 1969). The workshop’s score is a fixed, hand-weighted average of similarities with no probability behind it, so a score of 0.95 says nothing about how likely the pair is to be one person or how many errors a cutoff will make.
Why records with a unique ID are different. With a unique, reliable identifier, records can be merged exactly and there is no uncertainty about who is who to model; the paper’s method is for the common case where no such identifier exists and records must be compared on error-prone fields such as names, addresses and dates of birth (Enamorado et al., 2019). For those records agreement is only evidence, so the model estimates the probability of a match and carries that uncertainty into the analysis of the merged data instead of treating every link as certain.






Why the answer key matters.



Every number in this assignment is measured against the validation set, which the simulation makes for you. In a real project no such key exists. The assignment asks you to report how confident you are in the key itself, and to say what would have to be true for your conclusions to hold without it.


How confident I am in the key. The key is right by construction about which records were copied: TEA records 1–100 are copies of TRS records 1–100, and the other 400 TEA records were drawn independently. The question is whether anything in the data contradicts it.

agreement <- function(d) {   # exact agreement after standardizing, all 500 x 500 pairs
  list(
    last  = outer(d$trs$last_name_std,  d$tea$last_name_std,  "=="),
    first = outer(d$trs$first_name_std, d$tea$first_name_std, "=="),
    dob   = outer(as.numeric(d$trs$dob_std), as.numeric(d$tea$dob_std), "==")
  )
}
dob_near <- abs(outer(as.numeric(d20$trs$dob_std), as.numeric(d20$tea$dob_std), "-")) <= 1

is_key <- matrix(FALSE, nrow(d20$trs), nrow(d20$tea))

title: EPPS 6302 Methods of Data Collection and Production: Assignment 8
text:
2. Build
The functions below reuse the workshop’s own pieces (deterministic_linkage(), calculate_similarity_efficient(), the same date rule and score formula) and add three arguments: the weights, a threshold and a blocking rule. score_pairs() looks similarities up by matrix position rather than with sapply(), which is faster and keeps TRS in rows and TEA in columns, the orientation the handout’s debugging log warns about. The check after the functions confirms that it reproduces the workshop’s all_comparisons score for every pair.

ws_weights <- c(last = 0.40, first = 0.30, dob = 0.30)

dob_similarity <- function(a_dob, b_dob) {   # same rule as the workshop
  outer(as.numeric(a_dob), as.numeric(b_dob), function(x, y) {
    diff_days <- abs(x - y)
    ifelse(diff_days == 0, 1.0, ifelse(diff_days == 1, 0.95, 0.0))
  })
}

score_pairs <- function(a, b, w = ws_weights,
                        block = c("none", "first_letter", "letter_or_year")) {
  block <- match.arg(block)
  ln  <- ws$calculate_similarity_efficient(a$last_name_std, b$last_name_std)
  fn  <- ws$calculate_similarity_efficient(a$first_name_std, b$first_name_std)
  dob <- dob_similarity(a$dob_std, b$dob_std)

  pairs <- expand_grid(idx_a = seq_len(nrow(a)), idx_b = seq_len(nrow(b)))
  letter_a <- substr(a$last_name_std, 1, 1); letter_b <- substr(b$last_name_std, 1, 1)
  year_a   <- format(a$dob_std, "%Y");       year_b   <- format(b$dob_std, "%Y")
  if (block == "first_letter") {
    pairs <- filter(pairs, letter_a[idx_a] == letter_b[idx_b])
  } else if (block == "letter_or_year") {
    pairs <- filter(pairs, letter_a[idx_a] == letter_b[idx_b] |
                           year_a[idx_a]   == year_b[idx_b])
  }

  idx <- cbind(pairs$idx_a, pairs$idx_b)   # rows = TRS, columns = TEA
  tibble(
    record_id_a    = a$record_id[pairs$idx_a],
    record_id_b    = b$record_id[pairs$idx_b],
    last_name_sim  = ln[idx],
    first_name_sim = fn[idx],
    dob_sim        = dob[idx]
  ) %>%
    mutate(match_score = last_name_sim  * w[["last"]] +
                         first_name_sim * w[["first"]] +
                         dob_sim        * w[["dob"]])
}

run_linkage <- function(d, w = ws_weights, threshold = 0.95, block = "none") {
  det   <- ws$deterministic_linkage(d$trs, d$tea)
  comps <- score_pairs(det$remaining_a, det$remaining_b, w, block)
  prob  <- filter(comps, match_score >= threshold)
  links <- bind_rows(
    det$matches %>% select(record_id_a, record_id_b, rule_applied),
    prob %>% select(record_id_a, record_id_b, match_score) %>%
      mutate(rule_applied = "Probabilistic")
  )
  list(det = det, comps = comps, prob = prob, links = links,
       n_possible = nrow(det$remaining_a) * nrow(det$remaining_b))
}

# Precision, recall and F1 against the full answer key
assess <- function(links, key) {
  links <- distinct(links, record_id_a, record_id_b)
  tp <- nrow(semi_join(links, key, by = c(record_id_a = "trs_record_id",
                                          record_id_b = "tea_record_id")))
  fp <- nrow(links) - tp
  fn <- nrow(key) - tp
  precision <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else NA_real_
  recall    <- tp / (tp + fn)
  f1 <- if (!is.na(precision) && precision + recall > 0)
    2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) else NA_real_
  tibble(links = nrow(links), tp, fp, fn, precision, recall, f1)
}

# Label scored pairs with the key
label_pairs <- function(comps, key) {
  comps %>%
    left_join(key %>% transmute(record_id_a = trs_record_id,
                                record_id_b = tea_record_id, is_match),
              by = c("record_id_a", "record_id_b")) %>%
    mutate(is_match = replace_na(is_match, FALSE))
}


base <- run_linkage(d20)   # workshop settings
mine_scores <- base$comps %>% arrange(record_id_a, record_id_b) %>%
  select(record_id_a, record_id_b, match_score)
ws_scores <- ws$all_comparisons %>% arrange(record_id_a, record_id_b) %>%
  select(record_id_a, record_id_b, match_score)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(mine_scores, ws_scores, check.attributes = FALSE)),
